title: Clinical cases and practice
text: These are newly written teaching exercises, based on themes in Units 1–3, rather than copied questions from the lecture PDFs. They do not provide patient-specific medical guidance.

title: Clinical cases and practice
text:
Case 1: Grouping discrepancy
A patient’s forward and reverse grouping results are inconsistent.
Tasks: Identify the potential preanalytical, analytical and biological reasons to investigate; describe the laboratory checks that should take place before a group is assigned; state why issuing blood without resolving discrepancies can be hazardous.

title: Clinical cases and practice
text:
Case 2: Antibody history
A patient requiring red-cell support has a documented history of an anti-Jkᵃ antibody, but the current antibody screen is negative.
Tasks: Explain why historical records matter; identify the transfusion safety concern; outline the appropriate escalation within local pretransfusion-testing SOPs.

title: Clinical cases and practice
text:
Case 3: Pregnancy and anti-K
A maternal antibody investigation identifies anti-K.
Tasks: Discuss the importance of Kell antigens; compare the mechanisms of anti-K-associated fetal anemia with other HDFN mechanisms discussed in class; list issues requiring specialist coordination.

title: Clinical cases and practice
text:
Case 4: ABO inheritance
Two parents have genotypes AO and BO.
Tasks: Draw a Punnett square; enumerate possible genotypes and phenotypes in offspring; explain why routine blood grouping is a phenotype test rather than direct genotyping.






These are educational scenarios. Decisions for real clinical cases require validated laboratory results, local SOPs and authorized clinical oversight.

title: Unit 2: ABO, H and Secretor Blood Group Systems
text:
H and secretor loci
The Unit 2 slides distinguish the ABO locus (chromosome 9) from the H locus/FUT1 (chromosome 19). H antigen provides the precursor for A or B antigen expression on RBCs. The FUT2 secretor locus influences expression in secretions. The Bombay phenotype illustrates the importance of the H antigen pathway.

title: Unit 1: Foundations and Immunohematology
text:
Immunohematology essentials
Blood group antigens on red cells may be carbohydrate structures (such as ABO) or proteins (such as Rh). The immunological response to non-self red-cell antigens helps explain sensitization, antibody formation and the consequences of incompatible transfusion.

title: Unit 3: Other Clinically Significant Blood Group Systems
text:
Clinical interpretation
Clinical significance varies across antibodies. Consider antibody class, antigen prevalence, history of exposure and implications for compatibility and hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn. In particular, the supplied slides emphasize anti-K as important in both hemolytic transfusion reactions and HDFN, and Kidd antibodies in delayed transfusion reactions.
